newsitem.title: UK: Cool Britannia rules after London Fashion Week.
newsitem.headline: Cool Britannia rules after London Fashion Week.

text.p: The queen of punk rock paraded ravishing children in prim Scottish tweeds and supermodels wore bold British flags to propel London to the top of world fashion this week.
Forget Paris. Move aside Milan.

When London Fashion Week ends on Friday, experts say the innovative parade of wild hats, weird frocks and elegant clothes for real people will ensure Britain gets top billing in the global style stakes.
"English fashion designers are taking over the world. This is no blip -- London is producing clothes that simply everybody wants," said Katie Alers-Hankey, fashion coordinator for Tatler magazine.
"This week's show confirms London as a really cool, edgy place. It was floundering a few years ago but now the industry has forged an identity that works."
The identity is sassy yet stylish, practical yet fantastical, all part of a new-found confidence last seen in earnest during the swinging sixties.
From music to food to fashion, London is being touted as the happening capital of the world, part of a Cool Britannia trend that follows years of stagnation.
A record 350 overseas journalists came to town for this week's orgy of shows and British designers -- part of a four billion pound ($6.5 billion) industry -- are making their mark overseas too.
In an unprecedented coup in Anglo-French relations, Britons John Galliano and Alexander McQueen are now top designers at Dior and Givenchy respectively.
The august Italian house of Prada showed in London for the first time this week, while the U.S. magazine Newsweek crowned London "the world's coolest city".
New-fangled British pride displayed itself time and again on the catwalks.
Thighs were wrapped tight in the softest of mohair and plaid knickerbockers were paired with flat caps, sensible shoes and Argyle socks: as British as it comes.
Fantasy too was in abundance.

Amid sheets of dry ice, a shimmering snake-like creature curved seductively round the sculpted head of Yasmin Le Bon. Leggy Texan Jerry Hall emerged triumphant from under the floor in wickedly sexy ostrich feathers to ovations from her husband, Rolling Stone Mick Jagger.
Jagger was just another celebrity face in the throng, as Boy George (and his fuchsia felt trilby), the artist formerly known as Prince and all the bad boys of rock trooped in.
They, for once, were not the pull. It was the clothes, and the bodies in them.

Vivienne "Queen Viv" Westood, the 53-year-old who founded punk, stole the show by using nubile 13-year-olds to model her collection -- and saying nothing could be sexier for their onlooking fathers to watch.
Hardly surprising from the salty woman who made safety pins into an anarchist fashion statement and once visited Queen Elizabeth absent her knickers.

A regular in Paris and Milan, Queen Viv had shunned the London catwalks since 1990. True to style, the cult designer came over all churlish at her homecoming, proclaiming: "I am not patriotic. I don't like London."
Yet loud-mouthed Queen Viv and her shockingly demure clothes were home, proving Britain really is back.
"British fashion used to be weird but not wearable. Now it's wonderfully creative and commercial too. London may not have the chicness of Paris but it has an irresistible pull," said Alers-Hankey.
"After all, if you're not at the shows this week, you're really out of it."
